Apicurio Registry is a schema registry rooted in the Java ecosystem. It handles schema versioning, compatibility checks, and governance. But when a Python team needs to produce or consume Kafka messages in an environment where the Java team picked Apicurio, the tooling falls short.

The first instinct is the Confluent Kafka Python client. It has SerDes built in and can talk to Apicurio in some configurations. The problem shows up when the registry uses non-default artifact group IDs. Apicurio organizes schemas into groups, a namespace concept with no Confluent equivalent. If the Java team used custom group IDs instead of
, the Confluent Python serializers can't resolve the schemas. No configuration knob, no workaround.
That's the gap. A Python team needing to work with an Apicurio registry configured by someone else, on someone else's terms, had no ready-made solution.

Apicurio-serdes is a Python library that talks to the Apicurio Registry API directly. Artifact group IDs are first-class configuration: you specify the group, the library resolves the schema, the message goes through. No need to reconfigure the registry or fork Confluent's client to patch around its assumptions.

This library was written entirely by Claude. Not scaffolded or assisted, but designed, implemented, and tested through an AI-first process. I wanted to see what OSS looks like when the code is written by an AI and the human's job is to set constraints, review decisions, and push back.
